planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full to partial shade; give tall bugbane a permanent, sheltered site since it resents disturbance once established.

directions: Tall bugbane is a striking, shade-loving perennial native to lowland and foothill forests of western Washington and Oregon, where it grows in the same rich, consistently moist, humus-laden ground favored by big-leaf maple and western hemlock. In early-to-mid summer it sends up wand-like, branched racemes of small white flowers well above its broad, divided foliage, drawing in woodland pollinators during a season when little else blooms in deep shade. It is listed as a sensitive species in parts of its native range, so plant only nursery-propagated divisions and never collect from wild stands. Site it permanently in cool, sheltered, evenly moist shade, since established clumps dislike disturbance and take years to reach full size.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into consistently wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, and confine the planting with a buried barrier or container; giant horsetail spreads aggressively and is difficult to remove once settled into open garden ground.

directions: Giant horsetail is the tallest horsetail native to North America, forming dense colonies along shaded streambanks, seeps, and floodplain forest floors from British Columbia south through the Oregon Coast Range. In early spring, pale, unbranched, cone-tipped fertile stems emerge first and release spores before withering, followed by the taller, finely branched, bottlebrush-like sterile stems that persist through summer and give the plant its distinctive texture. It spreads aggressively by deep rhizomes, so it is best confined to a large container, pond margin, or an area already bounded by hardscape rather than open garden soil. Native peoples historically used the young fertile shoots as a spring food and the gritty, silica-rich stems as a natural scouring material.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall, 2-3 inches deep with the growing tip up, into moist, humus-rich lowland woodland soil in partial to full shade; this species has a narrow natural range, so purchase only nursery-propagated stock.

directions: Small-flowered trillium is a lowland Pacific Northwest native with a narrow natural range confined to moist forest remnants of the southern Puget Sound trough and the margins of Oregon's Willamette Valley, often growing alongside its more widespread relative Trillium ovatum in wetter, richer ground. It produces mottled gray-green leaves and a small, pale cream to greenish-white flower in early spring that ages toward a dull pink-purple as it fades, noticeably smaller and subtler than the showier wakerobins nearby. Like other trilliums, seedlings take several years to reach flowering size and resent root disturbance, so site permanent divisions in cool, humus-rich shade and leave them undisturbed. Its restricted range makes it a worthwhile but seldom-offered addition to a native rainforest-understory planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or bulblet offsets in spring into rich, constantly moist humus in deep to partial shade, mimicking the nurse-log and streambank microhabitats where this species naturally spreads.

directions: Small enchanter's nightshade is a diminutive, shade-loving perennial that marks genuinely old, undisturbed forest floor, spreading in loose colonies across damp humus and rotting nurse logs in coastal rainforest from Alaska south through the Olympic Peninsula and into the Cascades. Its heart-shaped, opposite leaves stay low to the ground, and in summer it sends up slender spikes of tiny, two-petaled pink-white flowers followed by small bur-like fruits that cling to passing animals for dispersal. It spreads gently by small bulblet-like offsets rather than aggressive rhizomes, making it a manageable, textural groundcover for the coolest, wettest, darkest corner of a woodland garden. Give it rich, constantly moist soil and deep shade for best results.
